questions.q: Why can't autoscaling alone fully absorb a sudden, severe traffic spike?
options: Autoscaling is only available on weekdays
The autoscaling control loop reacts on an interval and new replicas need time to load model weights, both of which can be outrun by a fast-moving spike
Autoscaling can only ever add exactly one replica regardless of demand
Kubernetes does not support scaling GPU workloads
questions.explain: Both the control loop's check interval and the cold-start time for a new replica introduce delay, and a genuine spike can grow faster than capacity can come online to meet it.

questions.q: What does admission control with a bounded queue do when the queue is full?
options: It silently drops requests with no response at all
It rejects new requests immediately with a clear error (such as 429), rather than letting the queue grow without limit
It shuts down the entire service
It automatically upgrades every request to a higher-priority tier
questions.explain: A bounded queue accepts requests only up to a fixed depth; once full, new requests get a clean, immediate rejection instead of unbounded queueing that would degrade latency for everyone.

questions.q: What problem do priority tiers address during a traffic spike?
options: They make every request process at exactly the same speed
They prevent one tenant's or client's burst of traffic from degrading the experience of other tenants sharing the same capacity
They eliminate the need for any rate limiting
They only apply to batch workloads, never real-time serving
questions.explain: Priority tiers (separate queues or rate limits for different traffic classes) keep one customer's spike from consuming capacity that other customers depend on.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of graceful degradation under load?
options: Permanently shutting down the service until traffic returns to normal
Falling back to a smaller, faster model or capping maximum output length so more requests can be served, even at lower quality
Ignoring the spike entirely and hoping it resolves on its own
Increasing the maximum output length for every request during a spike
questions.explain: Graceful degradation deliberately trades some quality or capability (a smaller fallback model, a shorter max output) for the ability to keep serving more requests under heavy load.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a per-client token-bucket rate limiter during a spike?
options: To guarantee every client gets unlimited throughput
To cap how fast any single client can send requests, so one client's burst doesn't consume capacity meant for everyone else
To permanently ban clients after their first request
To replace the need for autoscaling entirely
questions.explain: A token-bucket limiter bounds each client's request rate (with some burst allowance), protecting shared capacity from being monopolized by one client's spike.
